title: Teacher guide: Two Dreams
intro: The game follows a TeacherMind-style worksheet in which a student ice hockey player holds two dreams, sport and business studies, at the same time. It is a scaffold for discussion, not an assessment of the athlete.

ul: The purpose is not to decide the young person’s sports career or to assess athletic level.
The aims are to handle disappointment constructively, recognise strengths, strengthen belief in the future, build a dual career, find support in one’s network and practise perseverance.
The aim is not to give up the sporting dream. The aim is to add options.
Introduction, two situations (Season ends; On the bench), two dreams, and three closing questions. The situations can be done in either order.
There are eight stars. They come from doing the task, not from a particular choice.
Situation cards 12 and 13 and the ending were drafted from the teacher notes. Review the text before use.

sections.h: 3. What may lie behind the situation

ul: Being left out of the line-up or an injury can cause feelings of failure, shame, worthlessness, fear of the future and loneliness.
The student may not speak of these directly. Signs can be absences, late tasks, tiredness, irritability, lower motivation and withdrawal from the group.

sections.h: 4. The athlete is not the problem

ul: A goal-oriented athlete usually does not need easier demands but understanding, flexibility, individual guidance, clear goals and a chance to succeed.
Do not start with “Why are the tasks not done?”. Ask: “How are you right now?”, “How does the situation in the team affect you?”, “What support do you need?”
Find out: what the student aims for in sport, how the situation affects their thinking, which strengths they do not yet recognise and what support they need.
Highlight successes: “Did you notice how maturely you handled that situation?”, “Where else could you use this strength?”
Perseverance means taking the next step, breaking goals down, asking for help, tolerating disappointment and finding a new direction, not constant performing.
Ask: “What is the next small step?”, “What went well this week?”, “What can you be proud of right now?”
If the student learns at work, talk where possible with the workplace supervisor too: strengths, belonging to the work community, successes, motivation and realistic goals.
The work community can be an important support network when the young person feels outside the sports community. Do this with the student’s consent.

Make study-path options visible: vocational qualification in business, entrepreneurship, sports club marketing, event production, sales, coaching, sports business, pathway studies and university of applied sciences studies.
Ask the student: What is the next small step this week? Who can help? How will you know you succeeded? Answers are not stored.
Teacher’s own reflection (not in the game): stars of listening, trust, noticing, cooperation, hope and future-maker.
The teacher’s task is not to decide the young person’s future for them but to help see possibilities even when they see only a closed door.
If a student shares something worrying, follow your institution’s procedures. In an emergency call 112.
Progress is stored in the browser. On a shared device delete saved progress between users.
